prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identity of its active forms, which made incretin-based therapy of type 2 diabetes and obesity possible.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single prize part on B019 for Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, with the citation tied to GLP-1 physiology and its active forms. Round 1 showed that all six of us reached this trio independently, but I base my vote on the content: Holst's incretin and GLP-1 secretion physiology, Drucker's proglucagon-derived peptide biology and gut and islet actions, and Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active truncated peptide form a coherent discovery chain. That chain is confirmed by decades of independent work and by large randomized trials in type 2 diabetes and obesity, with cardiovascular and renal signals now accumulating. Maturity is not in question. The citation names discoveries, not liraglutide or semaglutide, which keeps the prize on the science and does not make a claim about the drugs themselves.
statement.case_against: The weak point is attribution, and round 1 did not remove it. Nobody, including me, can document from the material in front of us who first showed biological activity of GLP-1(7-36) and who first synthesized it. We all rely on recollection, and Mojsov's priority against the Habener group, who are not among the credited names, remains contested. Knudsen's exclusion under the three-laureate cap is a real cost, and I do not accept that splitting B019 into two parts would fix it, since the cap would still bind. B002 has the cleanest credit on the shortlist (Walter and Mori), and a prize there would be fully defensible. If the committee judged that a contested third name makes B019 fragile, that argument is legitimate and not a pretext.

responses.point: The chair asks what the committee does if the Mojsov priority question cannot be settled from the record, and whether it prefers Drucker, Holst and Mojsov with the dispute stated openly, Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, or a move to B002.
responses.response: I answer the sequence you asked for. First, the dispute cannot be resolved from this record, so I will not claim it is resolved. Second, my position is that unresolved is different from disproved: the specific step that bridges physiology to a therapeutic is the active truncated peptide, and Mojsov's role in identifying and synthesizing it is the best-supported reading of what I recall. I therefore keep Mojsov while the committee records the priority question openly in its reasoning. Third, if a committee check turned up primary publications showing the Habener group clearly first and Mojsov's work derivative, I would not default to Drucker, Holst and Knudsen. That swaps a discovery citation for a development one and weakens the logic of the prize. I would move to B002 before I rebuilt B019 around Knudsen. I do not support deferring B019 for sequencing, because nothing suggests B002 loses anything by waiting and nothing suggests B019 gains from delay except resolving a question that archival work may not settle.

responses.point: El-Manira moved B019 to first place in round 1 after ranking B002 first in the opening, while still calling B002 fully defensible, with mechanistic originality that GLP-1 cannot match, and listing the PERK and ATF6 contributions as an uncertainty for the Walter and Mori credit.
responses.response: I take your point on originality: the UPR is a conceptual discovery of the first rank, and I said as much in round 1. I would add that the PERK and ATF6 question is a weaker threat to B002 than the Habener question is to B019. Mori and Walter's identification of the signalling pathway from the ER to the nucleus is the discovery, and later mammalian branches elaborate it without displacing it. I still place B019 first because demonstrated benefit to patients at scale is a legitimate criterion, and the UPR's therapeutic path is not yet established. But your reasoning leaves me with a clearer fallback rule: if B019 attribution fails, B002 is the first choice, ahead of B004 or B008, and it would be a prize I could support with no reluctance.

responses.point: Perlmann asks why a credit difficulty is more tolerable for B004 than for B002, and warns that opening support for B019 should not be mistaken for resolved attribution.
responses.response: On your second point I agree: broad opening support for B019 reflects shared scientific judgment, not documentary verification, and I do not treat the count as a substitute for the priority question. On B004 versus B002, I do not think the credit difficulty is more tolerable for optogenetics. Six candidate names cannot be cut to three without a visible, arguable omission, whereas B002 has a compact pair with no obvious outsider. That asymmetry is why B002 is my first fallback and B004 my second alternative, not because I rate optogenetics' science lower. I would not accept B004 this year without a better answer on the trio than the committee has so far.

responses.point: Sandberg says the committee should reconsider, and not make the prize depend on Mojsov, if the evidence proves weaker than recalled, and treats anti-TNF as mature but a refinement of an already recognised paradigm.
responses.response: I agree on the conditional: the prize should not depend on a name whose priority we cannot support. Where I would go further is on what the committee should do in practice. Since no one can check the primary literature from the supplied material, the honest course is to state the uncertainty in the committee's reasoning and test the Mojsov and Habener question against the dated publications before the vote becomes final, and not to treat recollection as evidence. On anti-TNF I share your view that it is mature and important, but I would not place it above B002 or B004, since it extends a paradigm already recognised and I see no new argument from round 1 that changes that.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius says omitting Knudsen will be read as favouring academic discovery over development, and asks whether Habener should be considered even though not among the credited names.
responses.response: I agree the omission will be read that way, and the committee should own it. On Habener, I would separate two questions. The credited-name list is the evidence we were given, and I cannot add a person to a configuration on recollection alone. But I also cannot rule out that a better-documented credit would include him, which is why I list the priority question as my first uncertainty and not a footnote. For the citation, I propose language on discoveries of the physiology and active forms of GLP-1, which leaves room for the contributions of several groups to the identity of the active peptide, without naming a single step as exclusively one person's.

uncertainties: Whether primary publications and dates support Mojsov over the Habener group for identifying and synthesizing the active GLP-1(7-36) form; none of us can verify this from the supplied material.
Whether the exclusion of Knudsen and the drug-development arm can be stated openly in the committee's reasoning without implying the drugs were unimportant.
Whether a prize on B002 would be more robust than B019 if the Mojsov question were adverse, and how large an attribution risk the committee will accept before moving.
Long-term safety and durability of incretin therapy are still being characterized, though I do not treat this as a reason to withdraw support.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. My documented connections (co-authors including Sandberg, and the 2016 spatial transcriptomics paper) involve none of the credited names on B019, B002 or B004, and I request no recusal. Optogenetics is a neuroscience topic close to my field, but I have no documented personal tie to its credited names. I note the chair's flag that my co-authorship with Sandberg is documented and affects no shortlisted candidate.
